name: Clostebol (4-chlorotestosterone)

lead: Clostebol is testosterone with a chlorine atom added. It is sold in some countries as a topical wound-healing product, and bodybuilders have discussed it as an injectable ester for modest lean mass gains.

It activates the androgen receptor, and the chlorine is said to stop conversion to DHT and estrogen, which proponents link to a leaner, less puffy look. Its anabolic effect is described as modest. Published work is dominated by anti-doping analysis, and no trials test it for muscle or appearance.

paras: Physique users describe it as an injectable ester used in cycles, often alongside other compounds, with lean gains developing over weeks. In medicine it is a skin cream or spray for wounds.

Risks are inferred from anabolic steroids in general, as clostebol-specific human data for physique use are lacking. It is prohibited in sport, controlled in the US, Canada and Brazil, and some positive tests have been traced to accidental skin contamination.

angle.text: Clostebol is a chlorinated testosterone discussed for lean muscle support: it activates the androgen receptor with a mild anabolic effect and no DHT or estrogen conversion. The muscle use rests on class effects and user reports, and it is best known from skin creams and doping cases.

lead: Clostebol, also called 4-chlorotestosterone, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) derived from testosterone by adding a chlorine atom at the 4-position. It is usually formulated as an ester such as clostebol acetate, caproate or propionate.[1][2] In physique-enhancement circles, people discuss it as a testosterone-derived anabolic that might support strength and muscle, which in turn affects how muscular a body looks; a T Nation poster describes hearing it was good for strength and considering stacking it with other steroids.[3]

Its main legitimate uses are topical: clostebol acetate has been used in dermatological and ophthalmological products, and in some countries, including Italy, creams and sprays containing it are sold without prescription for minor skin wounds.[1] Because of that wide availability it is better known publicly through anti-doping cases than through bodybuilding. It is prohibited at all times by the World Anti-Doping Agency and appears regularly in doping cases, some attributed to accidental transdermal contamination, including the high-profile 2024 case of tennis player Jannik Sinner.[1][4][5][6]

No clinical trials have tested clostebol for physique or appearance. Older human trials examined it for other purposes, such as monocyte phagocytic activity and chronic hepatitis, and recent published literature is dominated by anti-doping analysis.[7][8][9]
infobox: US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV; Brazil Class C5; WADA-prohibited

paras: Clostebol acetate is used topically for infected or slowly healing skin lesions in some countries, often in combination with an antibiotic such as neomycin under the brand Trofodermin [1]. In Italy it is sold without prescription as a cream or spray for abrasions, fissures, burns and similar wounds [1]. Historical medical use of systemic forms has been reported for conditions such as osteoporosis, anorexia and wasting [2]. It has also been used illicitly as a growth promoter in cattle, which has led to residue surveillance [2].

T Nation threads from 2019 ask whether anyone has tried clostebol acetate and about Turinabol, which one member describes as structurally a cross between clostebol and Dianabol; in the same threads members state that the 4-chloro alteration makes the compound non-aromatising and without 5-alpha-reductase affinity [3][10]. These are forum statements, and no published trial supports them for physique outcomes.

The chlorine substituent is said to block conversion to dihydrotestosterone and to oestrogens [1]. Grokipedia gives an anabolic-to-androgenic ratio of about 46:25 relative to testosterone's 100:100 [2], whereas Wikipedia describes clostebol as a weak anabolic steroid [1]. Studies have characterised its urinary sulfate metabolites in a Caucasian population [11] and new metabolites for doping control [12], and a 2024 study examined how human keratinocytes and fibroblasts metabolise clostebol and five other anabolic steroids [13].

Clostebol is the 4-chloro derivative of testosterone with formula C19H27ClO2 [1]. A crystal-structure study of clostebol acetate established the absolute configuration of the ester and described it as used as an anabolic androgenic agent or applied topically in ophthalmological and dermatological treatments [14]. Oral Turinabol (chlorodehydromethyltestosterone) combines features of clostebol and metandienone and was used in East Germany's state doping programme, and methylclostebol is a reported additive in so-called dietary supplements [1].

Grokipedia reports that clostebol was first synthesised in 1956 as a halogenated testosterone derivative, with chlorine at C4 intended to modulate its anabolic-androgenic profile.[2] A 1964 German review discussed the 17-beta-acetate as an anabolic steroid.[15] Brand names include Steranabol, Macrobin and Trofodermin.[1]

Clostebol is also a structural parent of Oral Turinabol (chlorodehydromethyltestosterone). Wikipedia says the East German company Jenapharm patented that compound in 1961, that the idea of combining clostebol and metandienone came from chemist Albert Stachowiak, and that it was used in a secret state doping programme for about ten thousand East German athletes between roughly 1968 and 1989; it was in clinical use from 1965 until 1994.[16]

No studies found of clostebol for appearance or physique. A double-blind controlled trial of 4-chlorotestosterone acetate versus placebo measured the phagocytic activity of monocytes and found activity significantly higher in treated patients [7]. A 1975 controlled study of 66 patients with chronic active and fatty-liver hepatitis tested B vitamins and clostebol over eight weeks and found no demonstrable difference in chronic active hepatitis [8]. Recent human research is analytical, including a 2025 systematic review of seven papers covering 32 subjects on urinary clostebol metabolite after transdermal or transmucosal contact, which reported median M1 of 0.5 ng/mL after indirect exposure and 8.1 ng/mL after direct exposure [9]. Other work covers detectability after transdermal application of clostebol and several other steroids [17] and how clostebol positives may arise from accidental exposure [5][18].

Wikipedia lists numerous athletes suspended for clostebol, including baseball players Freddy Galvis (2012) and Dee Gordon (80 games, 2016), skier Therese Johaug (2016) and footballer Jose Luis Palomino [1]. A 2020 analysis said detections have grown, especially in Italy, because of wide availability of Trofodermin and more sensitive laboratory instruments, with most cases claimed to be non-conscious use or contact with relatives or teammates using it [5]. Another paper described incidental contamination after sexual contact [19].

Jannik Sinner tested positive twice for clostebol in samples from March 2024. An independent tribunal accepted that the substance entered his body through massages from his physiotherapist, who had used a clostebol-containing treatment on a cut on his own hand. On 20 August 2024 the tribunal found no fault or negligence, so no period of ineligibility applied, though he forfeited prize money and ranking points from the Indian Wells tournament.[6]

WADA appealed. In February 2025 the appeal was resolved by agreement: the positives were treated as inadvertent contamination, and Sinner accepted a three-month suspension from 9 February to 4 May 2025. WADA stated that an athlete bears responsibility for the negligence of his entourage.[6] The outcome drew public comment from players; Novak Djokovic said at the 2025 Qatar Open that many players felt there was favoritism toward top-ranked athletes, and Sinner's lawyer rejected what he called ill-informed commentary.[6]

A 2025 systematic review and other analytical papers examine how clostebol can appear in urine after transdermal or transmucosal contact, and how hair analysis and metabolite patterns are used to interpret positives.[9][18] A 2026 review of transdermal uptake of banned substances discusses the relevance for doping controls.[20] Researchers analysing the rise in positives, especially in Italy, point to the wide availability of Trofodermin and more sensitive laboratory instruments.[5]
